records.storyText:
Openai just launched their decisions endpoint, cloudflare launched clef the other week, and many more jev alternatives are out there.

We wanted to put the popular ones to the test and thought Pac-Man is a good benchmark for simple and fast decision making.

So we let jev 1.13, kev, clef, clef flash, GPT-6 Luna and Laya play Pac-Man against bot ghosts.

The low latency of these models allows for real time play. We had each model play 100 games, published a leader board and open-sourced the repo so anyone can run their own model and join the ranking. Link to repo: https://github.com/opper-ai/jevman-benchmark/blob/main/CONTR...

You can also join the game and play as Pac-Man yourself, and the ghosts are the models, either a mix of models or all jev, kev, clef etc. A game costs about 2 cent, all models are running via my startup opper, and we added free credits for everyone to try.

records.title: Show HN: Pocketty – iPhone SSH terminal that pings you when an agent is blocked
records.author: lukeed
records.storyText:
Hello~! pocketty is an SSH terminal for iPhone and iPad, made for herdr. herdr keeps your agent panes alive on your computer and knows the state of each one: working, needs you, or done.

I made this in anger/desperation for the latter half of my recent paternity leave. Nap traps are sweet, but there's only so much doom-scrolling and movie-watching I can handle... In any event, I've been using it for the last couple months and no longer have to be my desk anymore to be productive. Now the nap-traps are still productive (when i want them to be) !

How it works:

- The app talks to your computer directly over plain SSH. Tailscale is the easy way to reach it from anywhere but any SSH host you can reach works.

- A small Rust daemon on the host watches herdr. When a pane needs you, it seals the alert to your phone's key with HPKE (X25519, ChaCha20-Poly1305). A stateless relay (pocketty's) on Cloudflare Workers passes the sealed bytes to APNs (Apple Push Notification servers), and a notification extension opens them on the phone. The relay can't read them and keeps nothing.

- Your SSH key is made in the Secure Enclave and can't be exported.

- The terminal uses libghostty-vt for state and draws with wgpu on Metal, so full-screen TUIs look like they do on your desk, albeit narrower.

- Diffs for each agent turn, a file browser, and previews of `localhost` dev servers your agent starts, all through the same SSH connection. No port forwarding to set up.

herdr and the daemon are optional. Without them, it's a normal SSH client.

There's no account to set up and no analytics or tracking in the app. The app runs a 14-day free trial, with full feature access. Then, if you're as happy as I am with it, then it can be yours forever with a one-time purchase: $99 for the first two weeks (launch promo) then $129 after that.

Happy to answer anything about the sealed push setup or running libghostty on iOS.

records.title: Show HN: Layer – One API for Polymarket and Kalshi
records.author: pemakenemi56
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I'm David. I built Layer, an API + SDK or building trading bots/ai agents across prediction markets.

The idea came from something i kept running into while playing with trading bots. Once your bot needs access to more than 1 venue, you suddenly have to deal with different market schemas, contract definitions, prices, fees and APIs before you can reason about where to trade. That gets messy real fast, especially with prediction markets. The same real-world event can exist on Kalshi & Polymarket, but the contracts can be represented differently.

Here's my broader thesis: as more trading becomes automated, bots/agents will need a common interface to access different financial markets. Prediction markets felt like a good place to start because the fragmentation is obvious.

With Layer's SDK, you can: - pull normalized prediction-market data - match equivalent markets across Kalshi and Polymarket - compare prices across venues - see where a trade has a better payout - identify potential cross-venue arbitrage opportunities

Additionally, I built an example bot called Spread using Layer. It finds matched markets across venues and compares their prices after fees, so you can see which venue pays more for the same bet.

Layer is still super early and i would love your feedback, especially from people building trading bots/agents, or prediction-market tools.

Feel free to break it, build on it. Would love to see what you do with it.

records.title: Show HN: What a major earthquake does to Vancouver
records.author: tartieret
records.storyText:
About 10 years ago, I attended a presentation by someone who had compiled existing engineering reports to describe the impact of a major earthquake on infrastructure in British Columbia. It was really striking, and it has stayed in the back of my mind ever since.

I am now the point of contact for downtown Vancouver in the French community's emergency network, and it drives me nuts that most people I talk to have no emergency kit at home and basically no water.

People are shocked, or in denial, when I mention that it could take weeks to restore electricity and that they will have to rely on their own food and water for at least several days.

So I decided to build a public-facing site that compiles existing information, as a way to lay out the facts and help convince people, instead of hearing back that "the army will come" or that "there are emergency food reserves" (there aren't).

I see this as a citizen initiative, with one main message: go buy some water and canned food, it's your civic duty.

I relied on AI agents to compile the information, which is spread across hundreds of reports. With different levels of validation, plus my own review, I am confident the information is reliable, even if some details may not be fully up to date. The process took 2–3 weeks, alongside work, a toddler and a baby!

I'm posting it here because: 1) I'm curious to get feedback and suggestions. 2) Many HN readers are on the West Coast or in other seismic areas, so even if you're not in Vancouver, the general recommendations may be of interest. Be smart: buy some food and water.

Cheers

Thomas

records.title: Show HN: Client-side image cropping for any file input, without coding
records.author: rikschennink
records.storyText:
Hi HN!

We built CropGuide for people who don't code (or use platforms that don't allow custom code) but do want to improve the quality of images uploaded by their users.

To make that possible, we've built an admin tool where you configure your image requirements. Then you add a script tag to the page with the file upload field, either a standard file input or something more exotic powered by a library, and that's it.

The script catches images before they're added to the file input and lets the user edit them. Once edited, CropGuide places the resulting image back in the file input and everything continues as normal.

We really wanted to stay away from storing or processing images on our servers, so all of this happens client-side. Only the image requirements are fetched from the server.

Of course we're sharing because we're excited about having built and launched something new. Now it's fingers crossed that we can get some traction.

Would love to hear what you think!

records.title: Show HN: Wick, a daily word game where you guess by meaning, not spelling
records.author: jpage2
records.storyText:
Hello HN!

This is the first game I've ever made and I've been hooked on making apps/web apps ever since. At first it was closed-source for the first couple months of its launch, but this week I decided it should be made open-source. My reasoning for this is there are already a lot of games similar to mine that are about guessing a word based on the meaning of the word and narrowing down the secret word; but I added a little twist.

The game, "Wick", allows you to both narrow down the word by either 1. Guessing by meaning of the word like "fruit" is hot if the word is "lemon", or 2. Asking questions like "Is it a type of fruit?" and the Keeper will answer "Yes/No/Not Sure" etc... but will never spoil the answer.

It works by turning words into an embedding, which in simpler terms is a list of numbers that capture how the word is used semantically. Words used in similar ways get similar numbers. It comes from Gemini's embedding API for web/live race mode, but for iOS single player it uses free apple-intelligence on-device for the questions and it uses Apple's built-in English embedding and four small Core ML models for other languages like Spanish, German, Italian, and French.

The closeness of words is based on cosine similarity of two embeddings. The server embeds a vocabulary of 9,850 common words once, sorts them by closeness to the day's secret, and your guess is how close it is to rank 1 (the secret word). Rank 2 would be the closest word to the secret word. The categories of closeness are based on temperature so it goes: boiling, hot, warm, cool, cold, and freezing. At the end of the solve/game, you are rewarded with a semantic meaning map where it shows you all of your guesses and where they landed relative to the secret word as you narrowed in on it or gave up.

There's also no accounts at all, no ads, and no tracking of course. I pay out of pocket and am hoping to get users before I monetize or try to make money off the website. Right now I'm just hosting it for fun. I can do this because the vocabulary gets cached and there's only one embedding call per guess. It's one developer working on this app and web app. I'm receiving no funding currently for developing the game.

I wanted to copy osu!'s playbook a little, mostly because it's difficult for any game to maintain a moat or advantage over incumbents and have a reason to retain users. I thought that making it open-source and allowing people to contribute and add their own taste to the game would be nice. Also, I just enjoy making open-source code recently.

Play a few rounds please and let me know what you think or if you have any critiques to make it more fun/modular! I'd really like contributions if you're feeling up to it or comments/feedback on how I can improve!

Play it Live with no App Required: https://guesswick.com/

Source Code: https://github.com/jasonepage/Wick

iOS listing: https://apps.apple.com/app/id6777743483

records.title: Show HN: I used Claude Code to address the HN comments on my 2019 game
records.author: atum47
records.storyText:
In 2019 I posted Aim and Shoot here, a browser shooter where every enemy is a neural network evolved by a genetic algorithm between rounds: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=21353123

The thread had a lot of good feedback that I never got around to. This year I gave Claude Code the thread and the repo and worked through it:

- "Give the player full health every round" (four of you asked): done.

- "I wish there was a scoreboard, I wanted a screenshot of how far I got": the game-over screen now shows the round you reached and your best.

- "The gun sound is jarring": quieter, and M mutes it.

- "Enemies spawn on top of you and drag you around": bots now spawn at a safe distance, collisions are fixed, and there's a short grace period at the start of each round.

- "The bots all aim at the top-left corner, so camp bottom-right": this was a bug. Each bot only saw part of the game state. They now see every player, and aim, mutation and elitism are fixed too.

- "Kill the shooters first and the GA breeds pacifists" (by generation 8 they were running into walls): the fitness rewarded bots for living long, so your kill order picked who reproduced. It now rewards hitting you.

The biggest change came from a problem nobody quite named: evolution reset every time you died, so the bots never got far. Now there's one shared population on the server, and every round anyone plays moves it forward. Your browser only reports raw stats per bot; the server checks them, scores and breeds. It's PHP + SQLite on a small VPS, with a local fallback if the server is down.

It's at generation 1 right now. Whatever the bots are by tonight, you bred them.

Code: https://github.com/victorqribeiro/aimAndShoot

records.title: Show HN: APIblaze – Serverless MCP and API gateway with everything built in
records.author: jayjaychicago
records.storyText:
Hi HN. There are lots of API gateways out there. What we couldn't find was one with everything built-in to go from “my business logic works” to “I can safely consider publishing it on the internet”. So we spent a year building the features in APIblaze: A serverless MCP and API gateway. Here’s what makes it different:

- Authorization. Most gateways stop at authentication: they check who is calling. What they can and cannot do is left to your code or a plugin connecting to some sort of complex Authorization system. APIblaze provides users & groups management and enforces Authorization policies at the gateway, as a default suggested from your API spec. You add groups and write Authorization rules in plain English ("only whoever created a record, or an admin, can read or change that record"), tested and enforced by the gateway.

- Hosted end to end. APIblaze hosts the MCP server, the gateway, OAuth discovery and the login pages on the internet. One thing we really wanted to make easy was local development so the hosted API gateway forwards the requests to your backend, even if this backend runs on your localhost. So you can connect Claude/ChatGPT/… to the hosted MCP, bring your own oAuth and log into it (which is important because MCPs are all about taking actions and you have to know “who” is taking those actions), chat with your API to test it, and change your code live while the calls stream in your terminal.

- UI widgets: self-service API keys, users and groups and chat window. A drop-in React widget lets your users create, rotate and revoke their own keys on the developer section of your site. Another lets your customers' admins manage their own users and groups. A last one lets end users chat with your API on your App.

- Multi-tenant. Each customer gets its own keys, users, portal and MCP address to serve their own service to their end-users.

- The usual gateway tools: rate limits and quotas, transformations, custom domains and more.

- No lock-in: one command exports your setup (config, users, groups, and API keys as hashes so your callers keep theirs) to a runnable Kong bundle once you outgrow APIblaze.

To try it, paste this prompt into Claude Code or Codex, in an empty folder (you get a sample app) or in your backend's folder:

> Show me what APIblaze does using npx apiblaze skills

Or by hand, no sign-up needed:

  npx apiblaze create --target https://ninopizzas.com/openapi.yaml
It's in beta. I'd love your feedback, what you like and what you don't.

records.title: Show HN: CircleIt – Circle something on a web page, your coding agent fixes it
records.author: mintone
records.storyText:
Hi HN! Agents have made our development so much faster and we've found that the bottleneck has moved to feedback from the rest of the team. We have marketers and sales teams that were screenshotting pages and providing notes via Google Docs which then had to be translated to prompts by devs.

So we built CircleIt, a Chrome extension plus a Claude Code/Codex plugin. Anyone on the team can circle (and more!) things on any page (live/staging/dev), explain the change, and send it straight to the developer’s running agent. The screenshot, comment and meta information then goes straight to the agent. Then it makes the change and reports back, and the status updates in the sender’s browser.

Feedback is routed to the right repo by matching the site address, and you can require approval for specific people or sites before anything reaches the agent.

For us, small UI changes went from around a day of back-and-forth to a few minutes.

We’d love feedback - if this is useful then that's great!

records.title: Show HN: SpectroMood, speech emotion detection with a decision model
records.author: ketul_shah
records.storyText:
Voice AI industry still uses transcripts to determine the emotions of the user.

So when me and my friend were discussing about this we got the known limitations of transcriptions is that it doesn't capture the user's emotion from audio. Like, "I'm frustrated with your service" reads the same whether calm or angry.

Then I thought, why can't the decision model be tested for this to get quicker decisions on the go, knowing the limitation that it can't accept the audio file directly? So I thought of converting it to a pictorial representation and then submitting it to the clef-flash [a cheaper option]. Although the results are not too exciting, I would say it is just starting, and we can fine-tune the decision model for the same use case, and it can help a lot in several scenarios.

Worth giving it a try and checkout on your own voice.

records.title: Show HN: Streamline,recommendations from your watch history on streaming svcs
records.author: abhichandra21
records.storyText:
Streaming apps only recommend from their own catalogue, and only know what you watched on their service. Streamline reads the GDPR data exports from Netflix, Prime Video, Apple TV, Disney+ and Max, plus Plex plays, so it has your whole history.

How it works: each title is matched on TMDB and gets a short LLM-written description. From the titles you mark as loved, it builds a taste profile. The LLM tags each title once, and code groups them into themes, so the same ratings always give the same profile. A search turns your request into structured filters, gathers candidates from TMDB Discover and from LLM suggestions, removes everything you've seen, and ranks the rest against your request first and your taste second.

It's self-hosted (Docker, SQLite) and works with Claude, Gemini, OpenAI, or a local model. Searches cost about 6 cents with Claude. The docs screenshots are rebuilt by CI from a made-up library, so they never go stale and never show real data.

records.title: Show HN: Camp version controlled context workspaces
records.author: lancekrogers
records.storyText:
CLI tool for managing multi-project context workspaces in git with minimal effort and simple navigation.

Create a workspace with: camp create my-workspace

Convert an existing workspace to a camp: camp init

Give it a mission and a reason that it exists.

Load the shell integration with camp shell-init. Then csw my-workspace jumps to a workspace from anywhere on your machine. (Also supports switching between machines over tailscale with the same command)

Use cgo within a workspace to jump around your projects and context without typing long cd paths.

Commit your context from anywhere within the workspace with camp commit.

Add context linked commits to a project with camp p commit

Add -aw (auto write) flag to any commit command to write your commit messages in the background while you continue working.

records.title: Show HN: Claude Code spinner verbs reflect the model (Haiku: Licking screen..)
records.author: spaghettio
records.storyText:
I found it tricky to know which intelligence level (effort+model) my claude code is on so I used the claude mod system to make the spinner verbs depend on intelligence level and bake in jokes.

This plugin sorts the spinner verbs into six tiers by model + effort: Haiku gets "Licking the screen...", sonnet gets "Force-pushing to main...", Fable "Remembering the future..."

How it works: this is a 20 line registry file plus a 120 line verbs file. If you want to add custom verbs, modify verbs.ts. The only slighlty hacky workaround claude did was using hooks to identify the effort level since it's not exposed by the mods api. It takes the word claude code originally sampled and maps that to the word list.

Please send PRs with better verbs! Only rules: can't communicate something concrete about the code (like "Deleting and force pushing the codebase...", as that would make users lose their minds), and must correlate to model+effort level.
